primary_sources: Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, 1836

stimulus.text:
Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South (1836):

“But perhaps you will be ready to query, why appeal to women on this subject? We do not make the laws which perpetuate slavery. No legislative power is vested in us; we can do nothing to overthrow the system, even if we wished to do so. To this I reply, I know you do not make the laws, but I also know that you are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of those who do; and if you really suppose you can do nothing to overthrow slavery, you are greatly mistaken. You can do much in every way: four things I will name. 1st. You can read on this subject. 2d. You can pray over this subject. 3d. You can speak on this subject. 4th. You can act on this subject.”

Grimké added that laws forbidding Southerners to free enslaved people or teach them to read, “such wicked laws ought to be no barrier in the way of your duty.”

Background: Grimké was born into a slaveholding family in Charleston, South Carolina, and had moved north to join the abolitionist cause.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, The Anti-Slavery Examiner, September 1836, public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South (1836), public domain
stem: Why did Grimké appeal to women, even though she admits they 'do not make the laws'?

options.text: Women already held most seats in Congress
options.misconception: Women could not vote or hold office in 1836.

options.text: Women could reach the lawmakers, and read, pray, speak, and act
Women owned most of the enslaved people in the South
options.misconception: Grimké says nothing of the kind; she appeals to women as wives and mothers, not as owners.

options.text: Women were the only Southerners who opposed slavery
options.misconception: Grimké appeals to women because many had not yet acted, not because they alone opposed slavery.

rationales.A: Women held no seats in Congress in 1836. Grimké knows this, which is why she appeals to them differently.
rationales.B: They are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of lawmakers. They can reach the lawmakers, and they can act themselves.
rationales.C: The passage never says women owned most enslaved people. Grimké addresses them as family members of lawmakers.
rationales.D: Grimké is trying to wake her readers to action. If they already led the opposition, her appeal would be needless.
rationales.general:
1. Read Grimké's own question. She asks why she appeals to women who make no laws.
2. Read her answer. Women are the wives and mothers of the lawmakers, and they can read, pray, speak, and act.
3. Name the point. Power without a vote still counts, when it reaches the people who vote.
Remember: when a writer admits a weakness, look for the strength she offers instead.
